# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 35 POLITICS AT SEVEN GULLS

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

By the time Nell returned to the lower floor, a campaign before a general election was gripping both the Island and the whole of Canada. Being a passionate Conservative, Hugh was drawn into the commotion, as his presence was frequently requested to deliver speeches at several county rallies. Miss Winifred expressed her disapproval of his political involvement when she spoke to Nell.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0000 }

“Dr. Dave was never responsible for that. Dr. Carrow will discover that he has committed an error, trust ME. No respectable person ought to become involved in politics.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0001 }

“Shall the country’s administration be abandoned entirely to scoundrels, in that case?” inquired Nell.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0002 }

“Indeed—provided the scoundrels are Conservative,” stated Miss Winifred, departing with the victory. “Politicians and men in general possess the exact same faults. The only difference is that the Grits are coated far more heavily than the Conservatives—SIGNIFICANTLY more heavily. However, whether dealing with Grit or Tory, I counsel Dr. Carrow to avoid political affairs. Before anyone realizes it, he will be a candidate in a campaign himself, departing for Ottawa during six months of the year while allowing his medical work to fall into ruin.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0003 }

“Ah, well, let us not invite difficulty,” Nell remarked. “Its cost is far too steep. Rather, let us observe Little Kit. A G ought to be used to spell his name. Does he not look absolutely gorgeous? Look at the dimples in his elbows. You and I shall raise him to be a fine Conservative, Miss Winifred.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0004 }

“Raise him to become a righteous person,” Miss Winifred remarked. “Such men are rare and precious; all the same, remember, I would not wish him to end up a Grit. Regarding the vote, you and I can be grateful that we do not reside across the harbor. Over there, the atmosphere is foul currently. All the Kerrs, Crawfords, and MacAllisters have taken to the warpath, fully prepared for fight. Our side remains tranquil and quiet, given that men are so scarce here. Captain Saul belongs to the Grits, yet I believe he feels disgraced by it, since political talk never comes from him. Beyond any possible doubt, a massive majority will bring the Conservatives back into power once more.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0005 }

Miss Winifred had it wrong. Captain Saul stopped by the small home the morning following the election so he could share what had happened. Party politics contains a germ that is exceedingly poisonous, even to a quiet elderly gentleman, which caused Captain Saul’s cheeks to be red and his eyes to gleam with every bit of his former passion.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0006 }

“Mistress Carrow, a landslide victory has brought the Liberals to power. Following eighteen years during which the Tories misgoverned, this oppressed nation will finally be given an opportunity.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0007 }

“Captain Saul, I have never listened to you deliver a speech of such sharp partisan hostility until now. I was unaware that you possessed that degree of political malice,” chuckled Nell, who felt very little agitation regarding the news. Small Kit had uttered “Wow-ga” earlier that day. How could principalities and powers, the ascension and collapse of dynasties, or the defeat of Grit or Tory bear any significance when measured against such a wondrous event?
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0008 }

“A long while has seen its accumulation,” Captain Saul remarked, displaying a deprecating smile. “Only a moderate Grit was what I believed myself to be, yet upon receiving the news of our success, the true extent of my Grittiness became clear to me.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0009 }

“It is known to you that the doctor and I belong to the Conservative party.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0010 }

“Ah, well, that is the single fault I am aware of regarding either of you, Mistress Carrow. Winifred shares those Tory views as well. On my journey from the Glen, I dropped by to inform her of the news.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0011 }

“Were you unaware that you were risking your life?”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0012 }

“Indeed, yet I was unable to hold back from giving in to the urge.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0013 }

“In what manner did she react?”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0014 }

“Relatively peaceful, Mistress Carrow, relatively peaceful. She remarks, says she, 'Well, Providence dispatches times of mortification to a nation, just as to persons. You Grits have suffered cold and hunger for numerous years. Hurry to get warm and satisfied, because your time in power will be short.’ 'Well, now Winifred,’ I remark, 'perhaps Providence believes Canada requires an exceptionally extended period of mortification.’ Ah, Tabitha, have YOU received the word? The Liberals are elected.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0015 }

Tabitha had only recently stepped out of the kitchen, accompanied by the smell of delicious food that appeared to constantly surround her.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0016 }

“Now, are they?” she asked, displaying lovely indifference. “Well, I never could perceive that my bread rose with any less lightness when Grits held office than when they did not. And if a particular party, Mrs. Doctor, dear, can cause rain to fall before the week ends, thereby keeping our kitchen garden from being totally ruined, then that is the party for which Tabitha will cast her vote. Meanwhile, would you mind stepping outside for a moment to share your view regarding the dinner meat? I am afraid that it is extremely tough, and it seems to me that changing our butcher would be a good idea, just as changing our government would be.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0017 }

Seven days after that, when evening arrived, Nell journeyed to the Point in order to try to buy some fresh fish from Captain Saul, departing from Little Kit for her very first time. The event was a major tragedy. What if he began weeping? What if Tabitha lacked the precise knowledge of how to care for him? Tabitha remained untroubled and peaceful.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0018 }

“Is it not true, Mrs. Doctor, dear, that my experience with him matches yours?”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0019 }

“Indeed, with him—yet not with different infants. Why, three sets of twins were in my care when I was a youngster, Tabitha. Whenever they wept, I calmly administered peppermint or castor oil to them. Recalling the detachment with which I handled every one of those infants and their troubles seems rather strange today.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0020 }

“Oh, well, provided Little Kit weeping occurs, I shall simply place a hot water bag against his small belly,” Tabitha stated.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0021 }

“It shouldn’t be excessively warm, you see,” Nell stated with concern. Oh, was making the trip truly a prudent idea?
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0022 }

“Do not worry, Mrs. Doctor, my dear. Tabitha will never burn a little man. Bless him, he does not think of crying at all.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0023 }

Nell eventually pulled herself free and ended up taking pleasure in her stroll to the Point, passing through the elongated shadows cast by the setting sun. Captain Saul was absent from the lighthouse living room, which was occupied instead by a different individual—a good-looking, middle-aged fellow possessing a firm, smooth-shaven chin, whom Nell did not recognize. All the same, the moment she took a seat, he started conversing with her as confidently as if he were a long-time friend. Neither his words nor his manner contained anything improper, yet Nell felt somewhat offended by such unceremonious familiarity from someone who was an utter stranger. She gave chilled responses, offering only the bare minimum that politeness demanded. Undeterred, her fellow occupant continued speaking for a number of minutes before offering an apology and departing. Nell felt positive that she caught a glint in his eye, which irked her. Who could this person be? An elusive sense of familiarity attached to him, yet she was sure he had never crossed her path before.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0024 }

“Captain Saul, who was the person that just left?” she inquired, when Captain Saul entered.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0025 }

“Ambrose Kerr,” the captain replied.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0026 }

“Ambrose Kerr!” shouted Nell. “Oh, Captain Saul—it was not—yes, it WAS the sound of his voice—oh, Captain Saul, I failed to recognize him—and I acted very rudely toward him! WHY failed he to inform me? He had to have realized I failed to recognize him.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0027 }

“He would not utter a single remark regarding it—he would merely relish the jest. Do not be concerned about ignoring him—he will consider it amusing. Indeed, Ambrose has finally shaved away his beard and trimmed his hair. His political party has won, as you are aware. I failed to recognize him myself when I initially set eyes on him. He was present inside Carter Flagg’s store located at the Glen during the evening following election day, accompanied by a throng of people, anticipating the results. Around midnight the telephone message arrived—the Liberals had triumphed. Ambrose simply stood up and exited—he refrained from cheering or yelling—he permitted the rest to handle that, and I suppose they almost raised the roof of Carter’s store. Naturally, every Tory had gathered across in Raymond Russell’s store. There was not a great deal of cheering IN THAT PLACE. Ambrose proceeded directly along the street heading to the side entrance of Augustus Palmer’s barber shop. Augustus was resting in bed asleep, yet Ambrose pounded upon the door until he arose and came downstairs, desiring to learn the reason for all the noise.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0028 }

“Step inside your shop and perform the finest work you have ever accomplished, Gus,’ Ambrose said. 'The Liberals have won, and you will be haircutting a fine Grit prior to sunrise.’
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0029 }

“Gus was furious—partially due to being pulled from his bed, but mostly because of his Tory beliefs. He swore that he would refuse to shave anyone past midnight.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0030 }

“'Sonny, you’ll perform whatever I demand of you,’ Ambrose declared, 'or I’ll simply flip you across my lap and administer the type of thrashing your mother neglected to give you.’
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0031 }

“He would have carried it out, as well, and Gus was aware of it, because Ambrose possesses the strength of an ox whereas Gus is merely a dwarf of a person. Thus he surrendered, hauled Ambrose into the establishment, and set to work. 'Now,’ he states, 'I’ll give you a haircut and shave, but should you speak a single word to me regarding the Grits winning the election while I am at it, I’ll slit your throat using this razor,’ he states. You would not have imagined gentle small Gus capable of being so savage, would you? Demonstrates the effect party politics can have on a person. Ambrose remained silent, had his hair and beard trimmed, and returned home. As his elderly housekeeper caught the sound of him walking upstairs, she peered through her bedroom door to check if it was him or the farmhand. And upon spotting an unfamiliar man walking briskly down the hallway holding a candle, she shrieked hysterically and passed out completely. A doctor had to be summoned before she could be revived, and a number of days passed before she was able to gaze at Ambrose without trembling uncontrollably.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0032 }

Captain Saul had caught no fish. During that summer, his boat trips occurred rarely, and he had finished his lengthy walking journeys. A large portion of his time was passed beside his window facing the sea, gazing across the gulf, while his hand supported his rapidly blanched head. On this evening, he remained seated in that spot through numerous quiet minutes, maintaining a rendezvous with bygone days that Nell refrained from interrupting. Soon, he gestured toward the western twilight hues:
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0033 }

“Isn’t that lovely, Mistress Carrow? However, I would be glad if you had witnessed the sunrise earlier today. It was a marvellous sight—marvellous. Every sort of sunrise coming over that gulf has been seen by me. My travels have taken me across the entire globe, Mistress Carrow, and considering everything, a more splendid spectacle than a summer sunrise over the gulf has never been witnessed by me. A person is unable to choose their moment of death, Mistress Carrow—one simply must depart when the Great Captain issues His sailing orders. Even so, were the choice mine, my departure would happen as the morning moves across those waters. Numerous times I have observed it and considered how magnificent it would be to slip away through that immense white radiance toward whatever lay ahead on the other side, across a sea unmapped on any earthly chart. It is my belief, Mistress Carrow, that lost Margaret would be found by me over there.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0034 }

Ever since he had related the ancient tale to Nell, Captain Saul had frequently spoken to her about lost Margaret. In each inflection of his voice, his affection for her vibrated—an affection that had not once dimmed or lost its memory.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0035 }

“Regardless, I trust that when my moment arrives, my departure will be swift and gentle. I do not consider myself a faint-hearted man, Mistress Carrow—on multiple occasions I have confronted a gruesome demise without flinching. Nevertheless, contemplating a drawn-out end instills in me a strange, nauseating sensation of dread.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0036 }

“Do not speak of departing from us, dear, DEAR Captain, Saul,” begged Nell, her voice thick with emotion, caressing the weathered, dark hand, which had former strength, but was currently exceedingly frail. “How could we manage in your absence?”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0037 }

A lovely smile appeared on Captain Saul’s face.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0038 }

“Oh, you would get along fine—fine—yet you would not completely forget the old man, Mistress Carrow—no, I do not believe you will ever entirely forget him. People of Joseph’s race constantly remember each other. However, it will be a recollection that will not cause pain—I enjoy believing that my memory will not cause pain to my friends—it will always be somewhat agreeable to them, I hope and trust. It will not be very long from now until lost Margaret calls me for the final time. I will be completely prepared to reply. I merely mentioned this since there is a small favor I desire to request of you. Here is this poor old Matey of mine”—Captain Saul extended a hand and nudged the large, warm, velvety, golden sphere on the couch. The First Mate opened himself up like a spring while making a pleasant, throaty, contented noise, partly a purr and partly a meow, extended his paws into the air, rolled over, and rolled himself back up. “HE will miss me when I set out on the V’yage. I cannot endure the thought of leaving the poor creature to starve, as he was abandoned previously. If something occurs to me, will you grant Matey a morsel and a spot, Mistress Carrow?”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0039 }

“I certainly shall.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0040 }

“Well, that encompasses everything I wished to address. I have arranged for your Little Kit to receive the handful of unusual items I collected. Now, Mistress Carrow, it displeases me to witness weeping in such lovely eyes. Perhaps I will endure for a considerable duration still. Sometime during the previous winter, I overheard you reciting a poem by Tennyson. Should you be able to deliver it from memory, I would quite enjoy listening to it once more.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0041 }

While the ocean breeze drifted over them, Nell recited the lovely verses of Tennyson’s magnificent swan song—“Crossing the Bar”—in a quiet and distinct voice. With his lean, strong hand, the aged captain softly beat time.
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0042 }

“Yes, yes, Mistress Carrow,” he remarked, once she was done speaking, “that’s it, that’s it. You tell me he wasn’t a sailor—if he wasn’t one, I dunno how he could have expressed an old sailor’s emotions in words like that. He didn’t want any 'sadness o’ farewells’ and neither do I, Mistress Carrow—because all will be well with me and mine beyant the bar.”
{: #nw-v04-c35-p0043 }
